drills.prompt: {毎朝|まいあさ}、{公園|こうえん}＿{走|はし}ります。
drills.en: I run in the park every morning.

options.why: Running is an action that happens in the park → で.
に treats the park as a point you exist at or go to. Running is an activity, so it needs で.

drills.prompt: {京都|きょうと}＿{行|い}きたいです。
drills.en: I want to go to Kyoto.

options.why: Kyoto is the destination of 行く → に.
で would make Kyoto the stage for an action — "I want to go (somewhere), in Kyoto."

drills.prompt: {机|つくえ}の{上|うえ}＿{本|ほん}があります。
drills.en: There's a book on the desk.

options.why: ある is existence. Where something exists → に.
Nothing is happening; the book just exists there. で needs an action.

drills.prompt: レストラン＿{友達|ともだち}と{会|あ}います。
drills.en: I'm meeting a friend at a restaurant.

options.why: Meeting is an event that takes place at the restaurant → で.
会う uses に for the person you meet (友達に会う), not the place. レストランに会う would mean meeting the restaurant.

drills.prompt: {日本語|にほんご}＿{話|はな}してください。
drills.en: Please speak in Japanese.

options.why: The language is the means you speak with → で.
日本語を話す means "speak Japanese" (as a skill). Grammatical, but ください with を sounds like "please speak the Japanese language" rather than "say it in Japanese."
に has no "by means of" meaning.

drills.en: I get on the bus.

options.why: 乗る is getting onto/into something — the bus is where you end up → に.
バスで means "by bus," which needs a destination: バスで行きます. With 乗る alone it doesn't fit.

drills.en: I get up at 7.

options.why: A specific point in time → に.
で doesn't mark clock times.

drills.prompt: どうぞ、{部屋|へや}＿{入|はい}ってください。
drills.en: Please, come into the room.

options.why: 入る is entering — the room is where you end up → に.
で would mean doing the entering while already inside the room.

drills.prompt: {駅|えき}の{前|まえ}＿{待|ま}っています。
drills.en: I'm waiting in front of the station.

options.why: Waiting is what you're doing there → で.
に treats it as a point of existence or arrival. Waiting is an activity.

drills.prompt: {前|まえ}は{大阪|おおさか}＿{住|す}んでいました。
drills.en: I used to live in Osaka.

options.why: 住む is about where you exist/reside → に.
Tempting because "living" feels like an activity, but 住む is a verb of existence and takes に.

drills.en: I eat with chopsticks.

options.why: The tool you use → で.
に can't mark a tool or means.

drills.scene: Say you'll record at the harbor.
drills.en: I'll record at the harbor.
drills.why: Recording is an action at the harbor → で.

drills.prompt: もしもし、{今|いま}、{南口|みなみぐち}＿います。
drills.en: Hello? I'm at the south exit now.

options.why: いる is pure existence: where you are → に. Nothing's happening there yet, you just are there.
で needs an action. 南口で待っています works (waiting is something you do), but います on its own takes に.

drills.scene: On the phone with the person picking you up from the station.
Say where you bought your travel diary.
drills.en: I bought a diary at a bookstore nearby.
drills.why: Buying is an action that happens at the bookstore → で. を marks what you bought. The particle blocks can swap places; the verb stays at the end.

drills.prompt: {朝|あさ}ごはんは{一階|いっかい}＿{食|た}べます。
drills.en: Breakfast is eaten on the first floor.

options.why: Eating is an action, and the first floor is where it happens → で.
に would be for being on the first floor (一階にあります) or going there (一階に行きます). Eating needs で.

drills.scene: The inn staff explain the next morning while you check in.

drills.prompt: {富士山|ふじさん}は{日本|にほん}＿{一番|いちばん}{高|たか}い{山|やま}です。
drills.en: Mt. Fuji is the tallest mountain in Japan.

options.why: With 一番 ("the most"), で marks **the range you're comparing within**. Japan is the arena where the contest happens, the same "stage" idea as for actions.
に can't mark a comparison range. It would read as if the mountain were placed onto Japan.
日本の一番高い山 also works, but as a noun phrase ("Japan's tallest mountain"). With です after it, で is the everyday way to say it.

drills.prompt: {大学|だいがく}の{前|まえ}に{本屋|ほんや}があります。その{本屋|ほんや}＿{日記|にっき}を{買|か}いました。
drills.en: There's a bookstore in front of the university. I bought a diary at that bookstore.

options.why: Same bookstore, different job. In the first sentence it just **exists** (あります → に). In the second, buying **happens** there → で.
The first sentence's に is pulling you. に works with あります because the shop simply exists there; 買う is an action, so the place it happens takes で.

drills.prompt: {来月|らいげつ}、{東京|とうきょう}＿コンサートがあります。
drills.en: There's a concert in Tokyo next month.

options.why: The twist: ある takes に for **things** (本がある), but an **event** — a concert, a party, a meeting — is something that takes place, so its location takes で.
Logical if you think "ある → に," but that rule is for objects and buildings that sit somewhere. A concert happens, so Japanese treats the place as a stage → で.

drills.scene: The station is too far to walk with your bags. Say how you'll get there.
drills.en: I'll go to the station by taxi.
drills.why: Two places, two jobs: で marks **how** you go (by taxi), に marks **where you end up** (the station). The two blocks can swap; 行きます stays last.

drills.prompt: {名古屋|なごや}＿{電車|でんしゃ}を{乗|の}り{換|か}えます。
drills.en: I change trains at Nagoya.

options.why: Changing trains is an action that happens at Nagoya: で.
With 乗り換える, に marks the train you switch onto (新幹線に乗り換える). 名古屋に would make Nagoya the train.

drills.prompt: {夕方|ゆうがた}は{和食|わしょく}の{店|みせ}＿{食事|しょくじ}をします。
drills.en: In the evening I'll have dinner at a Japanese restaurant.

options.why: Having a meal is something you do there: で marks the stage.
に would treat the restaurant as a point you exist at or arrive at. 食事をする is an action, so で.
を already marks 食事. The restaurant isn't what you're doing.
